roots.context: We have learned that zero is the number for none, and that a 0 holds an empty place. Now we ask what zero tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In your test, a blank at the end of a number was missed, so 520 was read as 52. Numbers with a 0 written at the end, like 610, were read right. The 0 adds nothing to count, but it keeps the 5 and the 2 in their places. So a mark for 'none' does real work: it tells the other digits what they are worth.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'nothing' means 'doesn't matter', so it can be left out. But in a number, leaving out the mark for none changes the value of every digit beside it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the missing zero test, cards with a blank at the end were misread almost every time, and the same numbers with a 0 were read right. With the katoris, taking the empty katori away turned 205 into 25.

three.who_am_i: You can think about 'none', something you cannot see, touch or count on your fingers. Honeybees and crows seem to do it too.
three.what_is_life: A honeybee choosing between flower patches gains by telling 'some' from 'none'. Keeping track of what is missing helps a living thing as much as keeping track of what is there.
three.what_is_this_world: Nobody has ever found a place with exactly nothing in it. Even the emptiest space between the stars holds a few atoms and a little energy.

roots.thread: Ten digits, 0 to 9, can write every number there is. Zero is what makes this work, because it holds the empty places that give every other digit its value. Zero is also a picture of how everything begins. Before anything, there is a balance in which everything adds up to zero. From that zero comes One, and from One, the many, just as every number is built up from places that start empty.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at one hub, but it is the empty centre that makes the wheel useful. Shape clay into a pot, and it is the empty space inside that makes the pot useful.
teachings.link: The empty tens place in 205 is like the hole in the hub. It holds nothing, but without it the number does not work.

teachings.source: Isha Upanishad, opening verse (also Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1)
teachings.teaching: That is whole, this is whole. From the whole, the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: Brahmagupta's rule says that taking zero from a number leaves it as it was. The verse says something like it about the whole. It also points to infinity, the next unit.

teachings.source: Rig Veda 10.129, the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation)
teachings.teaching: Then there was neither being nor non-being. Who really knows how it all began?
teachings.link: The hymn asks what was there before anything. Scientists also ask whether any place can be truly empty, and nobody knows yet.

science.text: Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero in 628. His rules for adding, taking away and multiplying are the ones used today.
Even space with no atoms in it holds a tiny amount of energy, which physicists have measured. No perfectly empty place is known.
Whether bees and crows understand zero as a number is still argued about.

other_view.view: Zero is a tool people invented, like a word or a sign. It is very useful, but the jobs it does are rules we made up, not something we discovered in nature. On this view, it says nothing about where the world comes from.

practice.title: The pause between breaths
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly, all the way. Now wait a moment before the next breath. That small pause, with no breath going in or out, is a kind of zero. Let's do it five times. Then tell me: was the pause empty, or was something there?
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out all the way. Wait a moment before the next breath. Do it five times. Was the pause empty?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today. The missing zero test needs only chits, a pen and readers. A blank at the end of a number is invisible on plain paper, so the main result shows clearly: readers say 52 and 7 for cards meant as 520 and 700. Gaps in the middle give mixed results, which is worth talking about. The step says not to draw a line or box in the gap, because a box would act like a zero. If only one grown-up is at home, the cards can be sent as photos on WhatsApp. Readers who grow suspicious and ask 'is something missing?' are good evidence too. The ruler test depends on the ruler: most school rulers have a strip of 2 to 10 mm before the 0, and a ruler that starts at its edge gives a real 'no difference' result. The katori and bean activities need 20 dry beans, and beans must be kept away from children under 4. The abacus challenge uses pencils in atta dough, and a grown-up cuts any straws. Both games work for one child alone. Timings were checked step by step. The spine (intro, katori abacus, missing zero test, explanations, Brahmagupta's rules with beans, roots and quiz) fits about 90 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people used zero only as a mark for an empty place. Nobody added or multiplied with it. In the year 628, an Indian astronomer called Brahmagupta, who lived in Bhillamala in what is now Rajasthan, wrote a book called the Brahmasphutasiddhanta. In it he gave zero rules of its own. A number plus zero stays the same. A number minus zero stays the same. A number times zero is zero. These rules are still used today. But Brahmagupta also wrote that zero divided by zero is zero. In 1150, the Indian mathematician Bhaskara wrote that a number divided by zero is endless. Later mathematicians showed that both ideas fail a simple check. Division undoes multiplication: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 because 3 × 2 = 6. So 6 ÷ 0 needs a number that gives 6 when multiplied by 0. No number does, because anything times 0 is 0. And for 0 ÷ 0, every number works, so there is no one answer. Today mathematicians say dividing by zero has no answer.
how_we_found_out.who: Brahmagupta, an Indian astronomer and mathematician, and Bhaskara, who came about 500 years later
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Brahmagupta thought 0 ÷ 0 = 0, and Bhaskara thought a number divided by zero is endless. Checking division against multiplication shows that no number can be the answer, so dividing by zero is undefined.
